## USE GUIDE, DOCUMENTATION, BUILD FROM SCRATCH!!!

# OneTouch

Ask questions about the ServiceNow export in plain English, get the answers as tables,
download them in eight formats, and explore ten ITIL dashboards.

One computer runs the full tool (the **server**). Everyone else signs in to it with the
username and password they were given.

This file holds everything about OneTouch:

- **[Part 1: Using and running OneTouch](#part-1-using-and-running-onetouch)**: how to reach
  it, run your own copy, run the server, share it, set up dashboards and manage accounts.
- **[Part 2: Every feature, in detail](#part-2-every-feature-in-detail)**: what each part of
  OneTouch does, how it behaves, and its limits.
- **[Part 3: Building it from scratch](#part-3-building-it-from-scratch)**: 22 steps to
  rebuild OneTouch without cloning the repository, with every file printed in full in
  [Appendix B](#appendix-b-every-file-in-full).
- **[Branches and history](#where-each-branch-is)**: where each branch is and how the
  repository got here.

Keep it current: after any change to the code, run `npm run docs` and commit the updated
README. `npm run check` (about a second, with no Docker or API key needed) fails when this
file no longer matches the code, so run it before each commit.

---

# Part 1: Using and running OneTouch

## Using OneTouch from a clone of this repo (remote mode)

You don't need Docker, the data, or an API key. Your `localhost:8000` shows the tool
and passes everything to the OneTouch server, where your account lives.

1. Install [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 18 or newer.
2. In the cloned folder, run once:
   ```
   npm install
   ```
3. Ask whoever runs OneTouch for the **server address**, then start remote mode with it:
   ```
   npm run remote -- https://the-link-you-were-given.trycloudflare.com
   ```
4. Open **http://localhost:8000** and sign in with your own username and password.

Keep the terminal open while you use it, and press `Ctrl+C` to stop. You can put the
address in a `.env` file as `ONETOUCH_SERVER=...` and then just run `npm run remote`.
If port 8000 is busy, set `REMOTE_PORT=8100` (and open `localhost:8100`).

You can also skip all of this and open the server address directly in your browser.

## Running your own full copy (works without anyone else's computer)

1. Install Docker Desktop and clone this repo.
2. Copy `.env.example` to `.env`. Put an Anthropic API key in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`;
   the other values can stay as they are for a local copy.
3. Get the ServiceNow export (the six CSVs) from the team and put them in a `csv_data/`
   folder. Without them the tool still starts and you can sign in, but every question
   comes back empty. Add them before the first start, or see "Reloading the data".
4. Run `docker compose up -d` and open http://localhost:8000.
5. Sign in with your usual username and password. Everyone's accounts come with the
   repo in `db/accounts.json` and are loaded automatically.

**Getting account changes:** when someone is added, has their password reset, or is
deactivated, the person who made the change exports and commits `db/accounts.json`.
Pull, then restart your copy (`docker compose restart app`) to pick it up.

**Reloading the data:** the CSVs are only loaded the first time the database starts.
To load them later, run `docker compose down -v` and then `docker compose up -d`. This
also clears your copy's sign-in sessions; accounts come back from `db/accounts.json`.

## Running the server

Needs Docker Desktop, the CSV export in `csv_data/`, and a `.env` file
(copy `.env.example` and fill in every value). Then:

```
docker compose up -d
```

The tool is at http://localhost:8000. Nothing is reachable from other computers: the app,
Postgres, Cube and Metabase only accept connections from the server itself. Other people
use the Cloudflare link (https).

### Sharing it

**Over the internet.** Get permission first: this puts company data behind a public link.
One command starts OneTouch if needed, starts a Cloudflare Tunnel, checks the link works,
and copies it to your clipboard:

```
npm run share
```

The next section covers the one-time setup, what to do every time you start your computer,
and how to get a link that never changes.

### Sharing over the internet with Cloudflare

**How it works.** A small program in Docker (the `onetouch_tunnel` container) connects
out from your computer to Cloudflare. Cloudflare gives you a public `https://` link and
passes visitors through to OneTouch on port 8000. There are no router or firewall changes,
and the people you share with install nothing: they open the link and sign in with their
own username and password. Everything works through it: sign-in, the home page searches
and stars, the AI assistant, downloads, and the dashboards with drill-down.

It only works while **your computer is on and awake, with Docker Desktop running**.

**Changes reach people straight away.** Cloudflare tells browsers to keep script and style
files for 4 hours, so a browser could keep running an old `app.js` after OneTouch changed.
To prevent that, the server names each script and the stylesheet in the page with a version
made from its contents (`app.js?v=3fe9a193ee`). A changed file gets a new name, so browsers
fetch it on their next visit, and the page itself is never kept. This works for files added
the usual way (`<script src="x.js">`, `<link rel="stylesheet" href="x.css">`).

#### One-time setup

1. Install [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 18 or newer, and run `npm install` once in the
   project folder. This is what runs `npm run share`.
2. In **Docker Desktop → Settings → General**, turn on **Start Docker Desktop when you
   sign in to your computer**. OneTouch and the tunnel then start again by themselves
   after a restart.
3. In **Windows Settings → System → Power & battery → Screen, sleep & hibernate
   timeouts**, set **When plugged in, put my device to sleep after** to **Never**, and keep
   the computer plugged in. The screen can still turn off; only sleep stops the link.
4. Get the OK from whoever owns the ServiceNow data.

#### Every time you start your computer

1. Sign in to Windows and wait for Docker Desktop to finish starting (it says **Engine
   running**).
2. Open a terminal in the project folder (in VS Code: **Terminal → New Terminal**) and run:
   ```
   npm run share
   ```
3. Wait for **OneTouch is shared at: https://….trycloudflare.com**. The link is already on
   your clipboard: paste it to the people who use OneTouch. Before it prints the link, the
   command checks that the link works from the internet, so it's safe to send.

Why this is needed: the free link is new every time the tunnel starts, and the tunnel
restarts whenever your computer or Docker does. `npm run share` finds the current link,
and starts anything that didn't come back on its own. It's safe to run at any time; if
nothing restarted, it just shows the same link again.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run share` | Start sharing, or show the current link |
| `npm run share -- --new` | Replace the link with a new one (the old one stops working, e.g. to cut off people who had it) |
| `npm run share -- --stop` | Stop sharing; OneTouch keeps running on this computer |

Without Node.js, the same thing by hand: `docker compose --profile tunnel up -d tunnel`,
then `docker logs onetouch_tunnel` (the last `https://….trycloudflare.com` line is the
current link), and `docker compose stop tunnel` to stop.

#### A link that never changes (optional, about $10 a year)

A named tunnel keeps one address, e.g. `https://onetouch.your-domain.com`, through
restarts, so you never resend it. It needs a free Cloudflare account and a domain.

1. Create a free account at [dash.cloudflare.com](https://dash.cloudflare.com).
2. Buy a domain in **Domain Registration → Register Domains** (a `.com` is about $10 a
   year). Bought there, it's connected to your account automatically.
3. Go to **Zero Trust → Networks → Tunnels → Create a tunnel**, choose **Cloudflared**,
   and name it `onetouch`. If Zero Trust asks you to pick a plan first, choose **Free**
   (it may ask for a card even though it's $0).
4. On the install screen choose **Docker**, and copy only the long token that follows
   `--token`. Don't run the command it shows.
5. Add a public hostname (newer screens call it a *published application route*):
   subdomain `onetouch`, your domain, service type **HTTP**, URL `app:8000`. Save.
6. Add both lines to `.env`:
   ```
   TUNNEL_TOKEN=the-token-you-copied
   ONETOUCH_PUBLIC_URL=https://onetouch.your-domain.com
   ```
7. Run `npm run share`. With a token in `.env` it starts the permanent tunnel instead of
   the free one (and stops the free one), then prints your address once it's connected.

After that, a restart needs nothing from you: the tunnel comes back with Docker on the
same address. Running `npm run share` is still a quick way to confirm it's up.

#### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| `Docker is not running` | Open Docker Desktop, wait for **Engine running**, and run `npm run share` again. |
| `It is not answering yet` | A new free link can take a minute or two to start working. Open it yourself before sending it. If it still fails after 5 minutes, run `npm run share -- --new`. |
| People get "This site can't be reached" or a Cloudflare error page | Your computer is asleep or off, Docker isn't running, or they have an old link. Run `npm run share` and send the link it prints. |
| `The permanent tunnel did not connect` | The token in `.env` is wrong or was deleted in Cloudflare. Copy it again (step 4 above). |
| The permanent address shows "error code: 502", always or only sometimes | Something else is also running your tunnel: usually a container started by the dashboard's `docker run cloudflare/cloudflared … --token …` command, or the Windows service its `cloudflared.exe service install …` command creates. Those can't reach `app:8000`, and Cloudflare splits visitors between them and this project's tunnel. `npm run share` finds them on this computer and prints the command that removes each one: `docker rm -f <container name>` for a container, or, in an **administrator** PowerShell, `& "C:\Program Files (x86)\cloudflared\cloudflared.exe" service uninstall` for the service. The tunnel's **Connectors** list in the Cloudflare dashboard should show a single connector; one on another computer has to be stopped there. |
| A question shows an error after about 100 seconds | Cloudflare ends any request that takes longer than 100 seconds. It's rare (answers usually take 3–5 seconds); ask again. |
| Someone sees the old version after you change OneTouch | They press Ctrl+F5. Changes go live through the link as soon as they're running on your computer. |

**Limits.** Free links are a Cloudflare testing feature with no uptime promise; they're
fine for a team. Anyone with the link reaches the sign-in page, and only people with an
account in OneTouch can get past it.

### Presentation day (many people at once)

Measured with 30 people using OneTouch at the same moment, on the laptop that runs it:

| What 30 people do at once | How long each waits |
|---|---|
| Ask a question that was asked before | about 0.5 s |
| Ask a new question | 2–5 s, almost all of it Claude; the Claude API limits allow about 200 new questions a minute, and the cached instructions don't count toward them |
| Open the same dashboard | about 5 s (one person alone: 0.2 s), once the dashboards have been opened once |

A faster computer barely changes the AI answers: Claude runs on Anthropic's servers, and
OneTouch doesn't use a graphics card. Dashboards are the part a computer works hard on,
which is why Metabase keeps each chart's result (see [Dashboards](#dashboards-metabase)).

**On the morning of the presentation:**

1. Make sure OneTouch is shared: `npm run share`.
2. Warm it up:
   ```
   npm run warmup
   ```
   It signs in as the **warmup** account (username `warmup`, password from
   `WARMUP_PASSWORD` in `.env`, or it asks), then asks every question in
   `scripts/warmup-questions.txt` and opens every dashboard. The 55 questions cover
   incidents (priority, teams, channels, sites, on-hold, SLA breaches, causes, reassignment),
   problem records and parent / child tickets, changes (type, risk, failures, approvals,
   upcoming work, outages, SAP and breweries), approvals, requests and catalog tasks,
   whole-team views across ticket types, and one each of "nothing found", "outside the
   data's dates" and "not in the data". From scratch that takes about two minutes.
   To use another account instead: `npm run warmup -- --user <username>`.
   Afterwards those questions answer instantly for everyone, provided they're asked with
   the same words (capitals, spacing and a closing "?" don't matter), and every dashboard
   opens from Metabase's cache. It ends with a list of anything that failed, so it doubles
   as a final check that everything works.
3. Demo with the questions in that file. Edit the file to add your own (one per line) and
   run `npm run warmup` again; questions it has already asked come back instantly, marked ⚡.
4. **Don't restart OneTouch afterwards.** A restart (including `docker compose up` after
   editing `.env`) forgets the remembered questions. They are also tied to the date
   Claude sees as "today", which is the real date in UTC unless `ASSUME_TODAY` is set, so
   warm up on the day itself. A presentation that runs past 7 PM Central crosses into the
   next UTC day; run the warm-up again then.

Follow-up questions ("same but for changes") always go to Claude, so they take the usual
few seconds. The warm-up's answers list tickets like anyone's do, so they fill the Ticket
results of the account it signs in as. That is why it has its own **warmup** account: the
demo tickets land there, not in a real person's list.

**The warmup account** was created with
`docker exec -it analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs add warmup "Warmup"` and is in
`db/accounts.json`, so full copies of OneTouch have it too. Its password is `warmup`, which
anyone could guess, and OneTouch is on a public address. Anyone who tries it gets in and
can ask the AI questions (each new question costs a little). After the presentation,
consider `docker exec analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs deactivate warmup` (and
`activate` before the next one), or a stronger password with `reset-password warmup` plus
the same value in `WARMUP_PASSWORD`.

Keep the computer plugged in, awake and, if possible, on a wired connection.
Cloudflare serves the dashboards' 9.4 MB of program files from its own cache, so your upload
speed matters less than you might expect.

### Home page and the AI assistant

The header is one row: the OneTouch logo and name, the signed-in person's name, then the
**🏠 Home**, **📈 Dashboards** and **👥 Team** buttons, and right of them the **Ask Claude
about the data…** bar (the AI assistant, on every page). The button for the page you're on
lights up green (or in your own accent color; see [Making it your own](#making-it-your-own-colors-home-and-your-own-dashboards)).
**🔔**, **🎨 Colors** and **Sign out** are at the right. Clicking **Home**, the logo or the name
**OneTouch** goes back to Home from anywhere, closing the AI chat, the colors panel or the
dashboards drawer if one is open. On a phone, the buttons wrap onto more lines.

After signing in, people land on **Home**: "Welcome, *first name*!" in the top-left corner,
then their tickets: **📋 Assigned to me**, **📊 My charts** (the same tickets drawn as charts),
**👪 Team families** (project managers and admins), **Ticket results** and **Starred
tickets** (everything you've starred, newest first). Each person can add charts and
dashboard shortcuts with **✏️ Customize Home**.

**The AI assistant** is the **Ask Claude about the data…** bar in the header, right of the
**👥 Team** button, on every page (**/** jumps to it):

- Type a question in plain English, like "How many open incidents are there by priority?",
  and press **Enter** (or **💬 Ask**). The chat opens over the page with the answer. Ask
  follow-ups in the chat's own box.
- **💬 Ask** with nothing typed opens the chat, empty or with the conversation so far. A
  small count on it says how many questions the open conversation has.
- **A click anywhere outside the chat closes it**, the header included (a click on
  Dashboards, 🔔 or Colors closes the chat and does its own job at once). The conversation
  is kept. Windows opened from the chat (a ticket, a chart's tickets) don't close it.
- **Every full ticket number in the chat is a button** (INC, CHG, RITM, SCTASK or REQ and
  7 digits, in any case): in the questions you type yourself, in Claude's answers, in the
  text of an answer's tables and in the family notes under an answer. A click (or Enter)
  opens that ticket's record and family on Home, like a ticket number in a table.
- **A ticket that isn't yours** (another person's or another team's), clicked anywhere
  (the chat, a table, the ticket window, the Families page), says "🔒 You don't have
  permission to see …" and who can open it; nothing else about it shows. A number that
  isn't in the data at all still says "… is not in the data". Starred tickets you can no
  longer see are listed under the Starred list the same way.
- **🗑 Delete chat**, at the top of the chat, deletes the conversation. It
  asks first, then the questions and answers disappear, the assistant forgets the
  conversation, it leaves **Chat History**, and the chat closes ("Chat deleted"). An
  answer still on its way is dropped. **New chat**, next to **Ask Claude**, starts a fresh
  chat and keeps the old one under **Chat History**.
- **Chat History**, at the top of the chat, lists your saved chats, newest first. Click
  one to see its questions and answers again and carry on asking follow-ups; 🗑 deletes it.
- **Minimize** (or Escape) closes the chat and keeps the conversation.

**Every ticket list has a 🔍 Look up box** above it (Assigned to me, a family's tickets,
Ticket results, Starred tickets, the families in a ticket's record, the AI's answers, a
chart's tickets, the Team tab and the Ticket families page). It finds tickets by anything
their columns show: in **every column**, or in the one picked next to the box. Every word
typed must appear ("change high" finds changes with a high risk); "words in quotes" stay
together; a date can be typed as shown ("Sep 1, 2026") or as the data writes it
(2026-09-01). Lists shown a page at a time look through all of their tickets (the server
does it for the Team tab, Team families and the Families page). Escape empties the box.
The box remembers what's typed until you sign out.

**No cell is left blank.** Where the data has nothing, the cell says why (hover for more):
requests and catalog tasks show **No priority** (they have none in ServiceNow), a ticket
nobody was assigned **Not assigned**, a ticket with no parent **No parent**, and so on. A
request's **Team** is the team doing its catalog tasks ("No team (no catalog tasks)" when it
has none), and a request with no "requested for" shows who opened it ("*name* (opened it)").

**📊 My charts** draws the tickets assigned to you: by type, state, priority or risk, how
their KPIs look, when they were opened (week by week), and the ServiceNow team that worked
them. Pick open, closed or all; hover a bar or slice for its numbers; **▦** shows a chart as
a table; a click on a bar or slice opens **Assigned to me** with only those tickets (and
**✕ Show them all** to go back).

**Ticket results** is every ticket the AI assistant has shown you, newest first. When an
answer lists tickets, they appear at the top of the list automatically, highlighted, and a
note says how many ("28 tickets from this answer are now in Ticket results on Home"). Each
row shows the ticket's summary, its **Parent** and **Family** (see below), when it was shown,
and the question that showed it. A ticket shown again moves back to the top. The list is kept with your account (the
`seen_tickets` table in `onetouch_auth`), so it is still there after a refresh, after
signing out and in, and on another computer. Each person has their own list, holding the
2,000 most recent tickets.

Click a ticket number (in Ticket results or Starred tickets) to see that ticket's full
record: every field, with **Open in Dashboards** for incidents, changes and requests, and
**← All ticket results** to go back. A ticket opened this way also joins the list ("Opened
from a ticket number"). The list downloads like any other table.

**🧹 Clear ticket results** (at the right of the list's summary line) empties the list. It
asks first, and the list is then empty on every computer. Starred tickets stay starred, and
new answers start filling the list again.

**Ticking tickets.** Each row in Ticket results and Starred tickets has a checkbox (Shift-click
ticks a whole range, the box in the header ticks every row). The bar above the list then
offers, in this order:
- **💬 Ask the AI about *n*** opens a question box under the bar, with suggestions ("What do
  these tickets have in common?", "Which of these are still open?", "Who is working on these,
  and in which teams?", "Show me the full details of these tickets"). Type a question and
  press Enter or **Ask**, or click a suggestion. The chat opens and asks it as "About tickets
  INC1788698, INC1813985: *your question*" (up to 100 tickets at a time).
- **✕ Remove *n* from Ticket results** (in Ticket results) or **☆ Unstar *n*** (in Starred
  tickets).
- **☆ Unstar and ✕ remove *n* from Ticket results** does both at once, after asking, in
  either list.
- **Clear selection** unticks them.

Removing tickets leaves the rest, and their stars, alone; removing every row asks first,
like Clear ticket results. Ticks survive the list refreshing (after a new answer, for
example).

**Parent and Family.** Ticket results and Starred tickets both show, after the summary:
- **Parent**: an incident's parent incident, a request's bundle request (or, if it has
  none, its order, the REQ), a catalog task's request. Click it to open that ticket.
- **Family**: every family the ticket is in, with how many tickets each has, e.g.
  "Parent incident INC1813985 · 6", "Problem PRB0051839 · 96", "Order REQ0421352 · 18",
  "Change CHG1100098 · 2" (a change with the incident it fixes or the ones it caused),
  "Bundle request RITM0440455 · 3", "Request RITM0440498 and its tasks · 2". Click one to
  open its parent (or anchor) ticket, with the whole family under 🔗 Related tickets.
  Problem records themselves aren't in the export, so a problem isn't clickable.

These come from the same links as 🔗 Related tickets below, and are in the downloads too.
They are worked out once per ticket and then kept (the data never changes): 500 tickets
take about half a second the first time, a tenth of a second after that.

A ☆ appears next to every ticket number in OneTouch: in ticket results, in the AI assistant's
tables, and in the Dashboards toolbar on an incident, change or request record. Stars are
saved to each person's account (the `starred_tickets` table in `onetouch_auth`), so they
follow you to any computer that signs in to the same server. A full copy of the tool keeps its
own stars; they aren't in `db/accounts.json`.

**Unstarring many.** In **Starred tickets**:
- Tick rows (Shift-click for a range, the header box for all) and click **☆ Unstar *n***,
  or **☆ Unstar and ✕ remove *n* from Ticket results** for both (see Ticking tickets above).
- **☆ Unstar all** (at the right of the summary line) unstars every one, after asking.
- **Unstar by issue**: one button for each family that two or more of your starred tickets
  share, e.g. **☆ Unstar the 3 in Parent incident INC1813985** or **☆ Unstar the 2 in Order
  REQ0421352** (the biggest ten; a note counts the rest). One click unstars that whole group.

Each is one request, however many tickets. The ☆ on a single row still unstars just that one
and leaves the row (with an empty star) until the list is opened again, so a slip of the
mouse is easy to undo.

**Star all.** Ticket results, and every AI answer that lists two or more tickets, have a
row of yellow buttons: **★ Star all 30 tickets**, plus one per type when the list mixes
them (**★ Star all 28 changes**, **★ Star all 3 incidents**, **★ Star 1 request**, ...). Once
they are all starred, a button reads "✓ 28 changes starred". In an AI answer, it stars the
tickets the answer lists (its ticket-number column), not related numbers in other columns
such as a task's parent request. It is one request however many tickets there are, and the
2,000-star limit still applies: anything past it is left unstarred and a note says so.

**🔗 Related tickets.** Under an AI answer, and under a ticket's record on Home, OneTouch
lists the "families" those tickets belong to. These come from the links stored in the
ServiceNow export; nothing is guessed:

| Family | The link in the data | How common |
|---|---|---|
| Parent incident and its child incidents | `incident.parent_incident` | 2,080 child incidents under 514 parents (up to 212 children each; one level only) |
| Bundle request and its child requests | `sc_req_item.parent` | 1,543 child requests under 974 bundles (e.g. "Start and Snooze Applications/Servers" → "Virtual Server - Stop") |
| Requests ordered together | `sc_req_item.request` (the REQ) | 125 orders hold several requests (up to 18) |
| A request and its catalog tasks | `sc_task.request_item` | 2,361 requests have several tasks (up to 7) |
| A change and the incidents it fixes or caused | `change_request.incident`, `incident.caused_by_change` | 100 changes name the incident they fix; 6 incidents name the change that caused them |
| Tickets under one problem record | `incident.problem`, `change_request.problem` | 64 problems, up to 870 incidents each (the PRB records themselves aren't in the export) |

For each family it shows:
- a plain-English line on what the link means (e.g. "a parent (master) incident groups
  incidents raised for the same issue … so they are worked and resolved together")
- **Same in all** — the values every member shares: state, priority or risk, team,
  server / system, subcategory, catalog item, location, assignee, summary, opened time
- **Different** — the fields where they differ, with how many have each value (e.g. "Team:
  ACN-INFRA-CLOUD-LINUX (3), ACN-SAP-BASIS (3)", "Opened: Sep 1, 1:07 AM to 1:18 AM",
  "Summary: 5 different summaries")
- the members, each with its role (Parent, Child, Task, Incident it fixes, …). The
  ticket you asked about is highlighted. Up to 25 are listed, but the comparison covers all.
- **Download this family as** — the family in any of the download formats. The file has two
  tables: **Members of *anchor*** (every member, not just the 25 shown: ticket, role, type,
  summary, state, priority / risk, team, opened) and **Same or different in *anchor***
  (each field, "Same in all *n*" or "Different", and the values with their counts). The
  *anchor* is the family's parent, order, request, change or problem number. Table names
  start that way so they stay distinct as Excel worksheet names, which are cut at 31
  characters. When there are several families, **Download all *n* families as** at the
  top puts all of them in one file. The file is named after the tickets it relates to,
  e.g. `one-touch-related-to-inc1794145-2026-10-22.xlsx`.

One ticket shows every family it is in. A list shows only the families that two or more of
its tickets share, so a long list isn't buried.

**Opening a ticket shows its family first.** Whenever a ticket's record opens (a ticket
number in Ticket results or Starred tickets, its Parent or Family, a row of an AI answer, a
ticket in a family or in a chart's ticket list), its family comes right under its heading,
above the full record, headed "👪 *ticket*'s family: parent, children and other linked
tickets". Each family starts with a line saying where the ticket sits, and lists the parent
(or the order, request or change) on the first row:
- a parent: "INC1813985 is the parent incident. Its 5 child incidents are listed under it."
- a child: "INC1813970 is a child incident. Its parent is INC1813985 (the first row), which
  has 4 other child incidents." The parent comes first, then the child itself, then the others.
- also bundle and child requests, a request and its catalog tasks ("SCTASK0595823 is a
  catalog task of request RITM0440498 (the first row)"), an order, a problem record, and a
  change with the incidents it fixes or caused.

Big families show their first 25 members and **Show all *n***. A ticket with no family says
"No parent, child or other linked tickets". Ticket numbers inside a record (its Parent
Incident, Request Item, Caused by Change, …) and in AI answers are links too, so from a
child you can click straight to its parent and see the children. A ticket with no links shows nothing extra.
The families also go to the AI with your next question, so follow-ups such as "show me the
others in that family" work. The AI also knows these links directly: "child incidents of
INC1813985", "the parent request of RITM0440458", and an incident's record shows its
**Parent Incident** and **Problem Record**.

In child incidents, the parent's server / system matches 94% of the time, the subcategory
95%, the location 90%, the team 82%, the priority 75% and the state 99%. The summary
text matches only 9% of the time, because each alert or report carries its own detail.
Only about half the children were opened after their parent: the parent is the "master"
someone picked to group them, not always the first.

### Making it your own: colors, Home and your own dashboards

Each person can set up OneTouch their own way. Everything below is saved to their account
(the `user_preferences` table in `onetouch_auth`) as they go. It is all still there after a
refresh, after signing out and in, after the server restarts, and on any other computer.
Nobody else sees it.

**🎨 Colors** (header, right) opens a small panel:
- **Light or dark**: Light, Dark, or **Match my computer** (follows the computer's own
  setting, and changes with it).
- **Accent color**: OneTouch green (the default), blue, violet, pink, red, orange, teal,
  slate, or **＋** for any color at all. It colors the buttons, the lit Home / Dashboards
  button, and your charts. On a pale color, button text turns dark so it stays readable.
- **Header**: Dark (the default), the accent color, or the same as the page.
- **↺ Default colors** puts everything back.

The team dashboards switch to Metabase's own dark look when OneTouch is dark, and so does
every page a click inside them opens. Metabase's links can't know OneTouch is dark, so
OneTouch adds the dark look to each page as it opens, and **← Back** still steps back as
before. The accent color stays in OneTouch itself: Metabase keeps its own blue links, which
match OneTouch's.

**✏️ Customize Home** (next to the welcome) turns on editing:
- Each section gets **▲ Move up**, **▼ Move down** and **Hide**. The sections are
  **💬 AI assistant**, **🎫 Your tickets** (Ticket results and Starred tickets) and
  **📊 Your dashboards**, which is hidden at first and has one-click shortcuts to the
  dashboards you built. Hidden sections come back with their **＋** button.
- **＋ Add a chart** puts a chart of your own on Home (the same chart builder as below).
- **↺ Reset Home** goes back to the default (it removes the charts you added to Home, not
  your dashboards).
- **✓ Done** stops editing. Charts on Home keep their own buttons (see below) all the time.

**My dashboards.** At the top of the **☰ Dashboards** drawer, above the team dashboards:
- **＋ New dashboard** asks for a name and opens it, empty. **＋ Add a chart** adds charts,
  or **✨ Add suggested charts** fills it with a starter set: open incidents, open changes,
  open catalog tasks, incidents per day, open incidents by priority, changes by risk, the
  top catalog items, and open tasks by team. Change any of them afterwards.
- **✎ Rename** and **🗑 Delete dashboard** (it asks first) are above the charts, with
  **🔗 Share** (see below).
- **Filters for every chart** (the row under those buttons): **Opened** (any time, the
  data's last 7 / 30 / 90 days, or between two dates) and **Team** (pick one or more from
  every team in incidents, changes and catalog tasks, with a search box). They apply to
  every chart on the dashboard at once, on top of each chart's own choices, and are saved
  with the dashboard. Requests have no team, so a request chart ignores the Team filter and
  says so under it. **✕ Clear filters** removes them.
- Each person can have up to 20 dashboards of up to 30 charts each.

**Click a chart to see its tickets.** On any of your charts (Home, your dashboards, a
shared dashboard, and AI answers that are exactly a chart), a click on a bar, donut slice
or point of a line, or on a big number, opens a list of the tickets behind it (with the
dashboard's filters too): how many there are, the newest 200 with ☆ stars and **Star all**,
and a download. The tooltip says "Click to see these tickets". Click a ticket number to open
it in a window over the list: its family first (parent, children and other linked tickets,
as on the [Ticket families](#ticket-families-dashboards) page), then its full record. Its
parent and children open in the same window, with **← Back**; closing it returns to the list.
The keyboard works too: Tab to a bar and press Enter.

**Sharing a dashboard.** **🔗 Share** gives a link (**Copy link**). Anyone who signs in to
OneTouch and opens it sees the dashboard, with its filters, and can click its charts; **＋ Add
to my dashboards** gives them their own copy to change as they like. When you change the
dashboard, the link shows the change; copies people already added don't change. The button
reads **🔗 Shared** while it is shared; **Stop sharing** (in the same box) turns the link off,
and so does deleting the dashboard. Shared links live in the `shared_dashboards` table of
`onetouch_auth` (up to 20 per person).

**The tours.** On a first visit, a short tour of six steps points at Home and Dashboards, the
AI assistant, your tickets, Customize Home, Dashboards and Colors. The first time you open
the Dashboards page, it has a tour of its own (seven steps): the **☰ Dashboards** button,
then, with the drawer opened for you, Ticket families, your own dashboards, the team
dashboards and **Show or hide team dashboards**, then (drawer closed) clicking a team
dashboard for details, and the **❔ Tour** button. A step whose part isn't on screen is left
out (on the Ticket families page there is no team dashboard to click, so that tour has six
steps). **Skip the tour**, **Next** / **Back**, and Escape work in both. Once a tour is closed
it doesn't come back by itself (that is saved to your account, separately for each tour), and
**❔ Tour** shows it again: on Home for Home's, at the right of the Dashboards toolbar for
the Dashboards page's (just **❔** on a phone). Accounts that already existed see the
Dashboards tour once too, the next time they open Dashboards.

**The chart builder** has a live preview that redraws as you choose:
1. **What to count**: incidents, changes, requests or catalog tasks.
2. **Which ones**: All, **Open only** or **Closed only** (each ticket type's own states, shown
   under the buttons); when they were opened (any time, the data's last 7 / 30 / 90 days,
   or between two dates); and **＋ Only include some…**: up to six conditions. Each matches
   in one of three ways: **is one of** or **is none of** ("Priority is one of P1, P2"; every
   choice is listed with how many tickets have it, most common first, with a search box),
   or **contains** ("Team contains WINTEL"; type a word, or several separated by commas).
3. **Group by**: a field (priority, state, team, category, catalog item, risk, location,
   …), a period (day, week or month opened; month resolved, closed or planned to start), or
   nothing, for one total.
4. **Show it as**: columns, sideways bars, line, area, donut, table, or one big number.
   Then how many to show (top 5 to top 50; the rest add up in a note, or in "Other" on a
   donut), the order (biggest or smallest first, or by the groups themselves, ascending or
   descending: A to Z with P1 first and New before Closed, or the reverse; over time, oldest
   or newest first), the color, and the size (small, medium or wide). The top N are always
   the biggest; the order only changes how they're lined up.
5. **Title**: or leave it empty for an automatic one such as "Open incidents by priority".

Every chart shows a tooltip with the number and its share when you point at a bar, slice
or line (or tab to it). Its buttons appear when you point at it: **▦** shows it as a table,
**⇅** changes its order (the same choices as the builder's; on someone else's shared
dashboard, only for you, on that page), **⤓** downloads it (its numbers in any format, a picture of it, and PDF / Word / Excel with
the picture in them; see [2.5 Downloads](#25-downloads)), **✎** edits it, **◀ ▶** move it,
**📌** (on a dashboard) puts a copy on Home, and **🗑** removes it. A builder opened from a
dashboard with filters shows them under the preview, and the preview uses them.

**Hiding team dashboards.** **👁 Show or hide team dashboards** at the bottom of the drawer
turns each team dashboard into a checkbox; untick the ones you don't use and click
**✓ Done**. They disappear from your list only. The Dashboards tab opens on the dashboard
you had open last, team or your own, on any computer.

The charts count tickets straight from the data (`charts.mjs` builds every query itself
from these choices). "Open" means the same as in the AI assistant's answers. The team
dashboards count a catalog task as open by its *active* flag instead, so they show 6 fewer
open catalog tasks (824 against 830): 6 tasks are marked Pending or Work in Progress but
no longer active.

### Accessibility (♿)

The ♿ button in the header (and **♿ Accessibility** at the bottom right of the sign-in
page, or **Alt+A** anywhere) opens a panel of settings. They're kept in the browser, so the
sign-in page uses them too, and saved to the account, so they follow the person to any
computer. **↺ Default settings** puts everything back.

- **Text size:** 100%, 115%, 130%, 150% or 175% for every page.
- **Seeing the page:** high contrast (black on white, or white on black in dark mode),
  easier-to-read text (a plainer typeface with more space between letters, words and
  lines), bold word beginnings (like Bionic Reading: the first part of every word in bold,
  light, medium or strong; ticket numbers, codes like P1, text boxes, menus and charts are
  left as they are, and the page's text itself never changes, so copying, searching and
  read-aloud work as before), underlined links and ticket numbers, a strong yellow-and-black focus outline, a
  big mouse pointer, a reading guide (a band across the page that follows the pointer),
  and less motion.
- **🔍 Magnifier:** the text under the pointer shown large beside it (2×, 3× or 4×); with
  the keyboard, the box or button that has focus. A password box only says it's one.
- **🔊 Read aloud** (the browser's own voices): **Alt+R** reads what's selected, pointed at
  or focused (Alt+R again or Esc stops). Optional: a 🔊 Read button by selected text, Claude's
  answers read as they arrive, and reading whatever the pointer rests on. Every answer in
  the chat has its own **🔊 Read**; a table is read as its number of rows and its columns,
  and ticket numbers as their type and digits ("incident 1 2 3 4 5 6 7"). A voice and a
  speed can be picked, with **▶ Try it**.
- **🎤 Speak instead of typing:** 🎤 by the Ask bar and by the chat's box, or **Alt+M** in
  any text box (including the sign-in page's). What's said is typed where the cursor is;
  with **Ask Claude as soon as I stop talking**, the question is asked when they stop.
  The browser turns speech into text online (Edge through Microsoft, Chrome through Google),
  so it needs the internet and the person's permission for the microphone
  (`Permissions-Policy: microphone=(self)` in `server.mjs`). Firefox can't take dictation;
  the 🎤 buttons are hidden there and the panel says so.
- **Keyboard:** the first Tab on a page shows **Skip to the page**; `/` the Ask bar, Alt+A
  the panel, Alt+R read, Alt+M dictate, Esc stops reading or listening.

All of it is `public/accessibility.js` (one function, so none of its names can clash with
the other page scripts) and the "♿ ACCESSIBILITY" part of `style.css`; the settings are the
`access` part of the person's preferences (`prefs.mjs`, `cleanAccess`).

### The architecture map (admins only)

**🧊 Architecture** in the header opens a 3D map of how OneTouch is built. Only admins get the
button, and the server refuses the map's data to anyone else. On smaller screens the button
is just the 🧊.

- **Moving around:** drag to turn, scroll to zoom, Shift+drag or right-drag to move, or use
  two fingers on a touch screen. With the keyboard: arrow keys turn it, **+** and **-** zoom,
  **0** resets, Tab reaches each block's name and Enter opens it.
- **The blocks:** each floor is a layer of the stack, from the page at the top to Postgres at
  the bottom. The dashed frame is what Docker Compose runs on one computer, and outside
  services are outside it. Click a block for what it does, how it's protected, what it's
  connected to and where its code is.
- **What happens when…** follows a real request step by step: signing in, asking Claude,
  opening a dashboard, assigning a ticket, and the ServiceNow live push. The moving dots show
  which way data goes. They aren't live traffic.
- **📚 Tech stack** lists every version, read from `package-lock.json` and
  `docker-compose.yml`, so they can't fall behind.
- **📝 List** has the same content without the 3D, for screen readers and for a browser that
  can't draw 3D (which gets the list by itself). Colors follow each person's scheme, and ♿
  Less motion stops the dots, the slow turning and the camera moves.

**The ServiceNow live push is built, but it needs authentication from ServiceNow to work.**
The listener in `servicenow-sync/` is finished, and the map shows it as a dashed amber path
that stops at a locked gate. No data can arrive until:

1. someone with admin rights on the ServiceNow instance creates the system property, REST
   Message, Script Include and five Business Rules
   ([the blueprint](servicenow-sync/servicenow-blueprint.md));
2. the same secret is in ServiceNow's `x_onetouch.webhook_secret` and the listener's
   `WEBHOOK_SECRET` (ServiceNow sends it as `X-Webhook-Token`; without it the listener answers
   401 and saves nothing);
3. the listener is running at a public HTTPS address (it isn't in `docker-compose.yml`, and
   ServiceNow's cloud can't reach `localhost`), with its own database account.

The map says "needs authentication" until this server really hears a record, then it turns
green and shows how many have arrived. That count starts again whenever the server restarts,
and a test call with `curl` and the right secret counts too.

**Anything else that stops working is reported there too.** The banner lists each problem above
the ServiceNow notice, the block turns red, and **🩺 Health** shows every check, what a failure
means for people and how long it's been going on: sign-in and teams, ticket data through Cube,
Metabase, the Claude API, emails, the public address, the ticket-change channel, and any request
the server answered with an error in the last 15 minutes. Checks run only while the page is open
(`health.mjs`). **◀** minimizes the left side bar to the side, and **▶** brings it back.

What the map says is in `architecture.mjs`, because `public/` can be read without signing in.
`public/architecture.js` only draws it, with three.js kept unchanged in `public/vendor/`.
`npm test` fails if the map falls behind the repo: a file it names is gone, or a container in
`docker-compose.yml` isn't on it.

### Reporting a problem (🚩)

Anyone signed in can press **🚩** in the header, pick what kind of problem it is and say what
happened. Every admin is told straight away, under the 🔔 and by email (if they have an address on
file and haven't turned email off). The report goes with the person's name, the page they were on
and their browser. Someone can send 5 reports in 10 minutes.

The email only says who reported what kind of problem, like every OneTouch email: what they wrote
may name tickets or people, so it stays behind the sign-in, under the admins' 🔔 and on the
**🧊 Architecture** page. There the banner counts the open reports, and **📣 Reports** lists them for
an admin to mark resolved, or reopen. The sign-in page has no 🚩: reporting needs a sign-in.

### Ticket families (Dashboards)

**☰ Dashboards → Built into OneTouch → 👪 Ticket families** lists every family of tickets in
the data, from the links ServiceNow stored (the same ones as 🔗 Related tickets). It is part
of OneTouch, not Metabase, so it works the same for everyone and opens where you left it.

- **Six tabs**, each with how many families it has: **Parent incidents** (514, holding 2,080
  child incidents), **Bundle requests** (974), **Requests and their tasks** (12,880),
  **Orders** with two or more requests (125), **Problem records** (87) and **Changes and
  incidents** (106).
- **One row per family**, biggest first: the parent (or the order, problem or change), its
  summary, state, priority or risk, team, when it was opened, and how many it holds ("212
  child incidents"). Every column is filled in. An order or a problem record isn't a ticket,
  and a parent may belong to someone else (people only see their own tickets), so those rows
  are made from the family's tickets you may see: the commonest summary and team, each state
  with how many have it ("Closed (769), Resolved (95)"), the most urgent priority ("P2 - High
  (highest)") and when the first was opened, with a line saying so ("From its 18 requests").
  Click any heading to sort every family of the tab by it (the server sorts them all, not
  just the rows showing), again for the other way, and a third time for biggest first again.
  The 🔍 box looks up every family of the tab by any column. 50 rows at a time, then
  **Show 50 more**.
- **Click a row** to open the whole family under it: a line saying who the parent is ("INC1808293
  is the parent incident. Its 212 child incidents are listed under it"), what the members
  share and where they differ, the parent on the first row and every child under it (25,
  then **Show all**), and a download of the family.
- **Click any ticket number**, parent or child, in a row or in an opened family, to open that
  ticket in a window over the page: its family first (a child's says "Its parent is … (the
  first row)"), then its full record. Its parent, children and other linked tickets open in
  the same window, and **← Back** returns to the one before. **Open in Dashboards** shows the
  ticket's Metabase record page instead. An order's number opens the requests in it; a
  problem record isn't in the export, so it isn't clickable.
- **Find a ticket's families**: type a ticket number (INC, CHG, RITM or SCTASK) and **Find**
  to list every family it is in, whatever the kind. A single family opens straight away.

The lists are worked out once and then kept (the data never changes); `npm run warmup`
works them out in advance.

**On a ticket's record in a team dashboard** (an incident, change or request page, however
it was opened), OneTouch shows the ticket's family in a band above the page: one line
naming it ("👪 INC1813970's family: Parent incident INC1813985 and its 5 child incidents"),
then the same view as on this page, with the line saying who the parent is. The band
scrolls on its own so the record keeps most of the height, and **Hide family** folds it to
its one line (until you show it again). Click a ticket in it to open that ticket's record
in the same place (the band follows, and **← Back** returns); a catalog task or an order,
which have no record page, opens in the ticket window instead.

### Dashboards (Metabase)

Ten ITIL dashboards appear in OneTouch's **Dashboards** tab. Open them from the
**☰ Dashboards** drawer in its top-left corner:

| Group | Dashboards |
|---|---|
| Overview | IT Operations Overview, Sites & Breweries |
| Incidents & Problems | Service Desk, Problems & Major Incidents, Monitoring & Alerts, Workload & Channels |
| Change | Change / CAB, Change Risk & Business Impact |
| Requests | Requests, Automation & Self-service |

To create them on a server:

1. Fill in `METABASE_DB_PASSWORD`, `METABASE_ADMIN_EMAIL` and `METABASE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`
   in `.env`. If you already set up Metabase yourself, use that admin login.
2. Run `docker compose up -d`. This creates the reporting views and Metabase's read-only user.
3. Run:
   ```
   docker exec analytics_node_app node scripts/metabase-setup.mjs
   ```

Re-run step 3 any time. It rebuilds the dashboards in Metabase's "OneTouch ITIL"
collection and never touches anything else. The charts, and which drawer group each
dashboard sits in, are defined in `scripts/metabase-setup.mjs`. The data they read
is defined in `db/reporting-views.sql`.

**Caching.** The setup also tells Metabase to keep each chart's result instead of
recalculating it for every viewer, because the data never changes. With 30 people opening
the same dashboard at once, that took the wait from about 37 seconds to about 5. The
free edition only offers the "adaptive" policy, which keeps a result for 1,000,000 times
as long as its query took: about 14 hours for a 0.05-second chart, and about 11 days
for a 1-second one. The first person to open a chart after that waits the normal time,
and `npm run warmup` opens them all in advance. To switch caching on without rebuilding
the dashboards (which would change their links), run:
```
docker exec analytics_node_app node scripts/metabase-setup.mjs --cache-only
```

**Drilling down.** Click a bar, pie slice, line point, big number or blue table value
to open a detail page for it: a record (incident, change, request), a team, a server or
system, a site or brewery, a problem record, a catalog item, or a filtered list (e.g.
"Incidents · Priority: P2 - High"). Detail pages link onward too; on a record, use the
blue **Go to** row under it. OneTouch's toolbar shows where you are, with **← Back**, and
on a record, OneTouch shows the ticket's parent, children and other linked tickets above it
(see [Ticket families](#ticket-families-dashboards)). In dark mode every page stays dark.
A detail page's filter boxes (top left) suggest values as you type, so you can switch to
another team, ticket or item there. Clearing the last filter returns you to the dashboard.
What each click opens is set by `click` / `links` on the charts in
`scripts/metabase-setup.mjs`; the detail pages are its `DETAILS` list.

Metabase itself is at http://localhost:3000 on the server only. Everyone signed in to
OneTouch gets the dashboards, through links signed for them that show only the tickets
they may see (see [Teams](#teams-and-who-sees-which-tickets)): admins every ticket, a
project manager their team's, anyone else their own. There are no public links.

### Teams and who sees which tickets

Every ticket belongs to one of six teams, Example Team 1 to Example Team 6. Within its
team, each ticket is assigned to one person. What you see depends on your role:

| Role | Sees | Can |
|---|---|---|
| Admin (vperez, lvang, lbell) | Every ticket, and the Metabase dashboards | Put people on teams, set roles, move tickets between teams, assign any ticket |
| Project manager | Every ticket of their team | Assign the team's tickets to its members, and see who's working on what |
| Process excellence | The tickets assigned to them | |
| Project team member | The tickets assigned to them | |

This applies everywhere: the AI assistant (its counts are of the tickets you can see, and
a 👥 line under each answer says so), ticket search, records, Ticket families, and your
own dashboards. People on no team see no tickets.

**The 👥 Team tab** shows who's on your team and in what role. A project manager also sees
how many incidents, changes, requests and catalog tasks each person has, and every ticket of
the team with an **Assigned to** box on each (the 🔍 box above the list looks the team's
tickets up by any column: number, type, summary, state, family or who has it). Type part of someone's name (first name, last
name or username) and the team members who match drop down, each with their role and how
many tickets they have; pick one with the arrow keys and Enter, or a click. A click on an
empty box lists the whole team, "Not assigned" takes a ticket back, and Escape puts back who
had it. Tick tickets and type a name in **Give the ticked tickets to**, then **Assign**, to
hand out many at once. **Give all…** next to a family of linked tickets gives every one of
them to one person (after asking, since some may be someone else's), and so does the
**Give it all to** box on each family in Home's 👪 Team families. Whoever gets them is told
by the 🔔. An admin picks any team at the top, changes anyone's role or team in the people
table, adds people who are on no team, and can **Move tickets to another team** or give a
family to someone on its team.

**📥 Not assigned yet** (admins; first in the row of teams, with how many are waiting) lists
every ticket nobody has, whether its family is on a team or on no team yet (like the demo
tickets). Each family gets a row over its tickets: its first ticket's number and summary, how
many tickets of each type it holds, how many nobody has, and its team. From that row a family
on no team is moved to a team (it stays in the list, now with that team, until it's handed
out), and a family on a team is given whole to one of its people by typing a name; each ticket
also has its own name box. Families on no team come first. The Team and Type menus, the 🔍 box
and the column headings work as on a team's list (sorted by a heading, the family rows give way
to a **Move…** and **Give all…** link on each ticket).

**✅ Resolved or closed** (first on the Team tab, for admins and project managers) lists the
tickets someone said they resolved or closed, newest first: an admin sees every team's (with a
Team column), a project manager their own team's. Each row has the ticket, its type, summary
and state in the data, the status (with the member's note), who set it and when, who has the
ticket, and a **Change it to** menu: Resolved, Closed, or Open, which takes the status away
(after asking). The 🔍 box and the headings work as on every list. Only OneTouch's record
changes; the ticket's data never does.

**🎬 Before a presentation** (admins, at the bottom of the Team tab) puts things back the way
a presentation starts, each after asking: **↩ Undo every status** takes away every status
anyone set (and the 🔔 notifications that told project managers about them), and **🧹 Put the
demo tickets back** puts the 11 [Demo] tickets back on no team, assigned to nobody, with their
statuses, notifications, stars and ticket results gone, ready to move to a team and hand out
live. Every real ticket stays on its team, by family, with whoever has it. No restart needed.

**Clearing notifications.** Each notification in the 🔔 panel has a **Clear** button that
takes it off the list, and **Clear all** (next to the ✕ at the top) clears every one after
asking. Clear all only clears what the list was showing, so one that arrives at that moment
stays to be seen. Cleared notifications don't come back and no longer count on the bell; an
email already on its way for one still goes out.

**Notifications by email.** Everything the 🔔 shows is also emailed (`mail.mjs`), from
`notifications@onetouch.fyi` through Brevo: someone gets tickets (one email per hand-out,
however many tickets), a family is moved to a project manager's team, or a member says they
resolved or closed a ticket. An email says who did what and which ticket numbers, with an
**Open OneTouch** button; ticket summaries and a member's note stay behind the sign-in. Each
person turns it on or off with **✉️ Email me these too** at the top of the 🔔 panel (on by
default), which also shows the address. Addresses are set by an admin
(`docker exec analytics_node_app npm run users -- email <username> <address>`, or many at once
from a CSV with `emails -`) and live only in the database, never in `db/accounts.json`.
Test accounts and `warmup` are never emailed. A failed send is tried again (up to five
times) and never undoes the change; a notification more than an hour old when its turn
comes isn't sent, so switching email on later doesn't send old news.

To switch it on: in Brevo, authenticate the domain `onetouch.fyi` (its DNS records go in
Cloudflare) and add the sender `notifications@onetouch.fyi`; create an API key (SMTP & API →
API keys) and put it in `.env` as `BREVO_API_KEY`; restart the app. While `MAIL_ONLY_TO` in
`.env` lists addresses, only those are emailed: try it out that way, check with
`docker exec analytics_node_app npm run mail-test -- <address>`, then delete the line and
restart to email everyone. Brevo's free plan sends 300 emails a day.

**Families stay together.** Tickets linked to each other (a parent incident and its
children, a request and its tasks, an order, everything on one problem, a change and its
incidents) form one family, and a family always belongs to one team. So moving a ticket to
another team moves its whole family. Those tickets become unassigned, for the new team's
project manager to hand out. Someone taken off a team leaves their tickets behind,
unassigned.

On the first start the server sets the teams up by itself (`teams.mjs`): families go to
whichever team has the fewest tickets so far, and each ticket goes to a random member of its
team. Which role should work which kinds of tickets is being worked out in `CLAUDE.md`.

**New tickets from ServiceNow** (ready, waiting for access to an instance) follow the same
rules. A listener of its own, `servicenow-sync/` (`npm start` there, settings in its
`.env.example`), takes each record ServiceNow sends and saves it in the same table and
columns as the export. A new ticket joins the family of whatever it's linked to, and so that
family's team; one linked to nothing gets a family of its own on the team with the fewest
tickets. It arrives unassigned, in the team's "Not assigned yet". A ticket that links two
families merges them into the bigger one; tickets that change team that way become
unassigned, and that team's project manager is told. OneTouch picks the new tickets up by
itself: who sees them at once, KPIs, sorting and charts about 15 seconds later. What to set
up in ServiceNow is in `servicenow-sync/servicenow-blueprint.md`.

### Accounts

Accounts live in the server's own Postgres database (`onetouch_auth`). Manage them on the server:

```
docker exec -it analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs list
docker exec -it analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs add jsmith "Jane Smith"
docker exec -it analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs reset-password jsmith
docker exec -it analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs deactivate jsmith
docker exec -it analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs activate jsmith
```

To add many at once, use a CSV with the columns `Username, Display Name, Password` (PowerShell):

```
Get-Content people.csv | docker exec -i analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs import -
```

Never commit that CSV: it holds everyone's passwords.

**Sign-in links for everyone.** `node scripts/signin-links.mjs <people.csv> [address]` prints
one line per person (name, username, password, and a link that opens the sign-in page with
both filled in; see [2.1 Sign-in](#21-sign-in)), plus the test accounts and `warmup` from
`.env`. The output holds passwords: it only goes to your terminal, so copy each person their
own line and don't save, commit or post the list.

**Sharing accounts with clones.** After any change above, write the accounts file and commit it:

```
docker exec analytics_node_app node scripts/users.mjs export
git add db/accounts.json
git commit -m "Update accounts"
```

`db/accounts.json` holds usernames, display names and password *hashes*, never the
passwords themselves. Every copy loads it on start. Missing accounts are added, and an
account is only overwritten by a more recent change, so an old file never undoes a newer
password reset or deactivation.

## Coding helpers (Claude Code)

The repo includes two Claude Code subagents in `.claude/agents/`:

- **onetouch-developer** builds features. It knows how OneTouch fits together, how to run
  and test it, and the pitfalls this project has hit.
- **onetouch-reviewer** reviews a diff or branch for this project's risks (sign-in and data
  exposure, secrets, Claude API rules, setup that breaks on other machines). It is read-only.

In Claude Code, ask for them by name (e.g. "use onetouch-reviewer on my branch"), or see
them with `/agents`.

## Branches and checks

Everyone works on their own branch (`Ventura`, `Luke`, `Q`) and brings changes into `main`
with a pull request. Before each commit:

```
npm run docs     # refresh this file's appendices from the code
npm run check    # syntax, shell scripts, docker-compose.yml, and this file (about 1 second)
npm test         # Assigned to me's order against made-up tickets, and the architecture map against the repo
```

GitHub runs the same on every push and pull request (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`,
[B.79](#b79)), then checks that https://onetouch.fyi answers with OneTouch's sign-in page.
That last check fails whenever the computer running the tunnel is off.

---

# Part 2: Every feature, in detail

## 2.1 Sign-in

**The page.** Before you sign in, OneTouch shows only the sign-in page: the Molson Coors
logo, a box titled "Sign in to OneTouch", a **Molson Coors Email** field with
`@molsoncoors.com` printed after it, a **Password** field, and a **Continue with SSO**
button. Despite its label, that button signs in with the username and password stored in
OneTouch; it is not single sign-on.

- Type just the part before the `@`. Typing the whole address also works, because the
  server removes a trailing `@molsoncoors.com`. Usernames are not case-sensitive, and
  spaces around them are ignored.
- The **Microsoft Entra ID** button only shows "Microsoft Entra ID sign-in is not
  available yet. Use your email and password." The **Contact Support** link goes nowhere yet.
- After a failed attempt the password box is cleared and the error appears under it.

**Sign-in links.** A link like `https://onetouch.fyi/#user=jsmith&pass=secret` opens the
sign-in page with that username and password already filled in, so the person only clicks
**Continue with SSO** (or presses Enter). Encode anything unusual in a password
(`encodeURIComponent`). Details after `#` stay in the browser and are never sent to the
server or the Cloudflare tunnel, and the page takes them out of the address bar and the
tab's history as soon as it reads them. Opened in a tab where someone else is already signed
in, the link doesn't sign them out: a message says whose link it is, and the form is filled
in once they sign out. Anyone holding a link can sign in as that person, so give each person
only their own, and don't post the links anywhere shared.

**What the server checks** (`POST /api/login`):

| Situation | What you see |
|---|---|
| Wrong username or password | "Incorrect email or password." The server takes the same time whether or not the username exists, so it never reveals which accounts exist. |
| 5 wrong passwords in a row on one account | That account is locked for 15 minutes: "This account is locked for 15 minutes after too many wrong passwords." A correct password resets the count. |
| 20 failed attempts from one address within 15 minutes, across any usernames | "Too many failed sign-in attempts. Please wait 15 minutes and try again." Through the Cloudflare tunnel, the visitor's real address is used (taken from Cloudflare's header, and only believed when the request really came through the tunnel). |
| Deactivated account | Treated as a wrong password. |
| Account database unreachable | "Sign-in is unavailable right now (the account database could not be reached)." |

**Sessions.** A successful sign-in returns a random 64-character token. The browser keeps
it in the tab's `sessionStorage`, so:

- Reloading the page keeps you signed in. Your name is fetched again (`/api/me`), and the
  chat starts empty.
- Closing the tab, or opening OneTouch in a new tab, means signing in again.
- A session lasts 12 hours. After that, or after a password reset or deactivation, the
  next action returns you to the sign-in page with "Your session has ended. Please sign
  in again."
- **Sign out** (top right) ends the session on the server, clears the chat from the screen
  so the next person on that computer can't see it, and shows the sign-in page.
- The server stores only a SHA-256 hash of each token, and only salted scrypt hashes of
  passwords, so a copy of the account database can't be used to sign in. Expired
  sessions are deleted every hour.

## 2.2 The page around the tabs

- **Header:** one row with the OneTouch logo and name (click either to go back to Home), the
  signed-in person's display name (or their username if they have none), the **🏠 Home**,
  **📈 Dashboards** and **👥 Team** buttons, and **🧊 Architecture** for admins (the page
  you're on lights up in the accent color, green by default), the **Ask Claude about the
  data…** bar (the AI assistant), and
  **🔔**, **🎨 Colors** and **Sign out** at the right.
- **Home** is the first page after signing in: "Welcome, *first name*!" in the top-left
  corner, then your tickets (Assigned to me, My charts, Team families, ticket results and
  starred tickets; see
  [Home page and the AI assistant](#home-page-and-the-ai-assistant) in Part 1). Each person
  can reorder or hide those and add charts with **✏️ Customize Home** (see
  [Making it your own](#making-it-your-own-colors-home-and-your-own-dashboards)).
- **Colors:** each person's light / dark mode, accent color and header color, saved to
  their account. A reload starts in the colors this browser last used (kept in
  `localStorage` as `onetouch-theme`), so the default colors don't flash first.
- **Greetings** use the first word of the display name: "Welcome, *first name*!" on Home
  and "Hello, *first name*!" at the top of the chat.
- **Icons:** favicons, an Apple touch icon and a web-app manifest, so OneTouch can be
  pinned to a phone's home screen as "One Touch".
- **Tours:** a six-step tour of Home on a first visit and a seven-step tour of the Dashboards
  page the first time it is opened (each remembered per account), with **❔ Tour** on Home and
  on the Dashboards toolbar.

## 2.3 The AI Assistant (chat)

### Asking

Type a question in the **Ask Claude about the data…** bar in the header (on any page) and
press **Enter**. The chat opens over the page with the answer; ask follow-ups in its own box
(**Enter** or **Ask Claude**). A click anywhere outside the chat, **Minimize ▴** or Escape
closes it and keeps the conversation; **💬 Ask** with nothing typed reopens it.
**🗑 Delete chat** (at the top of the chat) deletes the conversation after a confirmation,
and Claude forgets it too. If you send
another question before the first answer arrives, it waits its turn: questions in one
session always run in order.

**Only your own tickets.** Every answer counts and lists only the tickets you have
permission to see (an admin's answers cover everything):

- **A question about tickets that aren't yours isn't answered.** "What is the state of
  CHG1099789?" gets "🔒 You don't have permission to see CHG1099789, so I can't answer
  questions about it", with no data. A question that names only such tickets isn't even
  sent to Claude; a follow-up that reaches one ("the second one") is caught once Claude
  has turned it into a query, and nothing is run.
- **An answer that leaves tickets out says so.** When tickets you can't see also match,
  a 🔒 note under the answer's first line says "You can't see the full report…" and what
  it covers ("Only the 153 tickets assigned to you are included"), or names the ticket you
  asked about that was left out. When nothing of yours matches but other tickets do, it
  says that instead. Downloads of the answer carry the same note ("Not the full report").
  When every matching ticket is yours, the answer is the full report and has no note.

**While it works**, a bubble shows each step as the server reaches it, with a running
clock: "📨 Sending your question…", "🧠 Understanding your question…" (Claude), "📊 Getting
the data…" (Cube), and for an empty result "🔎 Nothing matched; working out why…".
Finished steps stay listed with a ✓ and how long they took. Under each answer, a small line
says how long it took ("Answered in 2.9 s"). A new question usually takes 2–5 seconds,
almost all of it Claude; the data itself comes back in under a tenth of a second.

**Repeated questions are instant.** The data never changes, so when a question that
starts a conversation has been asked before, by anyone, OneTouch reuses Claude's earlier
translation (and, for an empty result, its explanation) and answers in about 0.1 seconds.
The bubble then shows "⚡ Asked before: reusing that answer…" and the answer says "⚡ Answered
in 0.1 s: this question was asked before". "The same question" means the same words,
ignoring capitals, spacing and a closing "?", asked about the same "today". Follow-up
questions depend on the conversation, so they always go to Claude. The server keeps the
last 500 such questions in memory; restarting it starts the list over.

### What happens to a question

1. **Claude translates it**, unless it is a repeated question (see above), in which case
   the earlier translation is reused and the steps below still run. The model is
   `claude-sonnet-5-5` unless `CLAUDE_MODEL` says otherwise, and it returns a structured JSON answer whose shape the API enforces: an `intent`, up
   to one query per table, a one-sentence restatement, and the list of assumptions made.
   The instructions (`business_logic.mjs`) describe the six tables, every column, the
   exact values coded columns hold, ITIL vocabulary, and worked examples. They are sent
   with prompt caching, so repeated questions cost less. Today's date is added to every
   question (or `ASSUME_TODAY`, see 2.9).
2. **The server checks Claude's answer** (`normalizeAndValidate`) before anything runs:
   - only known columns, the `count` measure, and these operators: equals, notEquals,
     contains, notContains, startsWith, endsWith, set, notSet, gt, gte, lt, lte;
   - each query uses columns from one table only, and each table appears at most once;
   - values for coded columns are corrected to their exact spelling (e.g. "p1" →
     `P1 - Critical`, "cancelled" → `Canceled` for changes), and each correction is added
     to the assumptions;
   - sorting only on selected columns;
   - lists without a limit get 50 rows; nothing returns more than 500.
   If the answer fails these checks, you see "I couldn't map that question onto the
   data: …", and Claude is told why on the next question.
3. **Cube runs each query** against the database, one per table, side by side. If Cube
   is still starting up, the server retries up to 3 times, 2 seconds apart.
4. **Empty results are explained** (see 2.4).
5. **Counts across several ticket types are merged** into one table with a column per
   type and a total (`combineResults`). For "top N" questions, the server ranks the
   merged totals, so it's a true top N across all types.

### The three kinds of answer

| Intent | When | What you see |
|---|---|---|
| `query` | The question fits the data | The results (below) |
| `clarify` | It can't be answered sensibly without one more detail, e.g. a person's real name (people are anonymized as "Individual 1234"), or a place that matches very different things | 🙋 and one short question back |
| `unsupported` | It needs something the data model doesn't have: averages, durations, resolution times, SLA %, joins between tables, or a period with no data | 🙋, a plain explanation, and the nearest question it *can* answer |

### What a result looks like

- **A title:** Claude's one-sentence restatement of what it fetched.
- **One number** ("how many open P1s") → a big number with the right noun ("12 incidents").
- **One record** with more than 4 fields (a ticket lookup) → a two-column field / value card.
- **A list or breakdown** → a table with a row count above it. Long text (descriptions,
  notes, plans) is cut at 120 characters, with the full text on hover.
- **Clickable ticket rows:** in a table that lists tickets, each row has a ▸ by its ticket
  number. Click the row (or focus it and press Enter or Space) and a detailed view opens
  under it:
  - the ticket's **full record**: every field, ☆ Star, **Open in Dashboards** for incidents,
    changes and requests, and a download
  - its **🔗 related tickets**: each family, with what the members share and where they
    differ, and the family downloads

  Click the row again or **▴ Close** to fold it away. Several rows can be open at once.
  While a row is open, the table shows in full instead of in a short scrolling box. The
  star in a row stars without opening it. **Open in Dashboards**, or a ticket number
  inside a family, closes the chat and shows that page.
- **Counts across ticket types** → one table: the grouping column, one column per type,
  a Total column and a Total row. Without grouping, it's a big total plus a row per type.
- **Lists across ticket types** → one titled table per type (25 rows each unless you
  ask for more).
- **Readable values:** column names in plain English ("Assigned Team", "Server / System",
  "Times Reassigned", "SLA Breached", "Parent Request (RITM)"), dates like
  "Aug 14, 2026, 8:44 AM", months like "August 2026", weeks like "Week 33 of 2026",
  true / false as Yes / No, empty values as "—", and counts with thousands separators.
- **How I read your question:** a collapsible list of every assumption Claude made (what
  "open" meant, which ticket types were included and why others were dropped, the exact
  dates used, values that were corrected).
- **🔗 Related tickets:** when the answer's tickets have parents, children or other linked
  tickets, the families they belong to, with what the members share and where they differ
  (see [Home page and the AI assistant](#home-page-and-the-ai-assistant)).
- **Star all:** when the answer lists two or more tickets, buttons to star them all, or all
  of one type (see [Home page and the AI assistant](#home-page-and-the-ai-assistant)).
  The tickets also go to Ticket results on Home.
- **Show as (charts):** an answer that counts things by one field or period ("open incidents
  by priority", "requests per month") has a **Show as** row: **Table**, **Columns**,
  **Sideways bars**, **Donut** and **Line** (or **Line**, **Area** and **Columns** for
  periods). Click one to redraw the answer that way, and **Table** to go back. An answer that
  compares ticket types ("requests and incidents per week") offers **Line**, **Columns**
  (side by side) and **Stacked columns**, with a legend, and one tooltip that reads every
  type at once; a total per type offers columns, bars or a donut. More than 30 categories:
  the biggest 30 are drawn and a note gives the rest (all of them stay in the table). Every
  chart has a tooltip on each bar, slice or point.
- **Click a bar for its tickets:** when the answer is exactly a chart (the server's
  `chartable` says nothing was left out), a click on a bar, slice or point of its chart
  lists the tickets behind it (see [Making it your own](#making-it-your-own-colors-home-and-your-own-dashboards)).
- **📌 Save as a chart:** on an answer that counts one ticket type by one field. It opens the
  chart builder filled in from the answer (the same ticket type, grouping, open / closed
  states, conditions and dates), in the chart type showing, with **Save to**: your Home
  page, one of your dashboards, or a new one. A condition a chart can't hold (for example
  "summary contains password") is named at the top, and the chart counts without it.
- **Download as:** see 2.5. Every kind of answer downloads, including a question back or
  an explanation of something the data can't answer, and, while a chart is showing, a
  picture of it.

### What it understands

The data is six ServiceNow tables. Four are **ticket types**: incidents (INC), changes
(CHG), requested items (RITM) and catalog tasks (SCTASK). The other two hold approval
records for changes and for requests.

- **"Tickets" means all four types.** "How many tickets came in last week" runs four
  queries and merges them. Approval records are included only when you ask about
  approvals. A request and the tasks created to fulfil it count as separate tickets.
- **Filters only go where they exist.** Priority, impact, urgency, category and channel
  exist only on incidents; type, risk, environment, outage and planned dates only on
  changes; catalog item on requests and tasks; team on incidents, changes (owning team)
  and tasks; location on incidents and requests. Types without the field are left out,
  and the assumptions say so.
- **Ticket numbers** (INC…, CHG…, RITM…, REQ…, SCTASK…) pick the table instantly, and a
  bare number shows that ticket's full record.
- **Answer shape:** "how many" → a count; "by / per / breakdown" → grouped counts;
  "top N / busiest / worst" → top N (10 by default); "trend / per month / weekly" → counts
  per day, week or month in date order; "show / list / which" → a list, newest first;
  "details / status of" → one record. "Percent / share" returns the counts and says
  percentages must be worked out from them.
- **Status words:** "open / backlog / pending / still open" → each type's open states;
  "closed / done" → each type's closed states ("resolved" alone → Resolved); "stuck /
  stale / aging" → open and older than 7 days; "on hold / waiting on the user / vendor";
  "reopened"; "bounced around / reassigned"; "failed / rolled back / caused an incident"
  for changes; "rejected"; "pending approval"; "fulfilled"; "SLA breached".
- **Priority words:** P1 / critical / sev1 / "on fire" → P1; P2 / high / urgent; "high
  priority" → P1 and P2; P3 / medium / normal; P4 / low / minor; impact words such as
  "enterprise-wide", "site down", "single user"; "was a P1 at some point"; "downgraded".
- **Time phrases:** "today", "yesterday", "last week" (Monday to Sunday), "this month",
  "last month", "last 30 days", "since July", "Q3", "YTD", "recently" (7 days); "resolved /
  closed / planned / went live in…" use those dates instead of the creation date. "Ever /
  all time" means no date filter.
- **Teams, places and things:** team nicknames map to the codes in the data ("wintel" →
  `WINTEL`, "service desk" → `ServiceDesk`, "Accenture" → `ACN-`, "TCS" → `TCS-`, and
  about 20 more). Brewery and office names, "HQ", "UK", "Canada" and "remote" map to
  locations. Server or app names match the configuration item. Plain words map to
  categories ("password / locked out", "printer", "VPN", "slow") and catalog items
  ("new laptop", "shared mailbox", "admin rights", "termination"). Channels such as "called
  in", "chat", "portal" and "monitoring alerts" are understood too.
